items.prompt:
Read this text below.

Ben the bunny loved carrots. He found one in the garden. He ate it all up.

Is this a fiction story or an informational text?

steps: Ben the bunny is a named, made-up character. He does things in a story. This is fiction, not real information about bunnies.

items.prompt:
Read this text below.

The sky is blue,
The grass is green,
The prettiest day
You've ever seen!

Does this text rhyme? What type of text is it?
items.answer: Yes, it rhymes. It is a poem.

steps: 'Green' and 'seen' rhyme. It is written in short lines. These are features of a poem.

items.prompt:
Read this text below.

The Earth goes around the sun. It takes one year to go all the way around. That is why we have 365 days in a year.

Is this text fiction or informational?

steps: This text gives real facts about the Earth and the sun. There are no characters or made-up events. It is an informational text.

items.prompt:
Read this text below.

The dragon flew over the mountains.
His wings were red as fire.
He searched for a cave to sleep in,
For his old bones were growing tired.

Is this a fiction story or a poem? Give two reasons.
items.answer: This is a poem. Reason 1: It rhymes (fire/tired). Reason 2: It is written in short lines arranged in a stanza, not in paragraphs.

steps: 'Fire' and 'tired' rhyme at the end of lines. The text is arranged in four short lines, which is a poem structure. Even though it has a character (the dragon), it does not develop a full story with a beginning, middle, and end. It reads as a poem.

items.prompt:
Read these two texts.

Text A: Aisha found a tiny egg in the garden. She kept it warm. One morning, a baby turtle crept out.

Text B: Sea turtles lay their eggs on sandy beaches. The eggs hatch after about 60 days. The babies crawl to the sea right away.

Which is fiction and which is informational? What is one difference between them?
items.answer: Text A is fiction. It has a named character (Aisha) and story events. Text B is informational. It gives real facts about sea turtles. One difference: Text A tells a made-up story, while Text B teaches true facts.

steps: Text A: Aisha is a character, the egg hatching is a story event. Fiction. Text B: gives facts (sandy beaches, 60 days, babies go to sea). No characters. Informational. Key difference: one entertains with a story, the other teaches with facts.

items.prompt: A student is reading a book to find out how rainbows form. Should they choose a fiction story or an informational book? Explain why.
items.answer: They should choose an informational book. An informational book will give real facts about how light and water droplets create rainbows. A fiction story might have a rainbow character or a magical story, but it would not give accurate scientific facts.

steps: Purpose matters when choosing text type. The student wants to learn a real fact (how rainbows form). That requires an informational text. A fiction story would not give accurate science. Matching purpose to text type is an important skill.

items.prompt:
Read this text below.

A drop of water falls from a cloud,
It taps the leaf so soft, not loud.
It soaks down deep to roots below,
And helps the tallest sunflower grow.

A student says: 'This is informational because it explains the water cycle.' Is the student right? Explain.
items.answer: The student is not fully right. The text does mention things that relate to how water reaches plant roots (part of the water cycle), but the way it is written (rhyme, short lines, poetic language like 'taps the leaf so soft, not loud') makes it a poem. A text can mention real processes and still be a poem based on how it is structured and written.

steps: The content touches on water movement and plant growth, which are real facts. But content alone does not determine text type. The rhyme (loud/loud implied with cloud/loud), short lines, and soft imagery are all poem features. An informational text would explain the water cycle plainly and completely. This text evokes a feeling about rain. It is a poem that happens to mention real-world processes.

items.prompt:
Read these two texts.

Text A: The snow fell all night. In the morning, Marco ran outside. He made a snowball and threw it at the fence. It exploded into a hundred white stars.

Text B: Snow forms when water vapor in clouds freezes into ice crystals. Each snowflake has a unique six-sided shape.

Which is fiction and which is informational? Explain what each text does that the other cannot. Why might a reader choose one over the other?
items.answer: Text A is fiction. It has a character (Marco), a setting, and events. It describes a snowball exploding into 'white stars,' which is poetic, not scientific. Text B is informational. It explains how snow forms with real facts. A reader who wants to feel the fun of snow would enjoy Text A. A reader who wants to understand snow scientifically would choose Text B. Each does something the other cannot.

steps: Text A creates a vivid scene. 'Hundred white stars' is a creative description of snow breaking apart. It is evocative and fun. Text B defines terms, explains a process, and states scientific facts. Neither text can do what the other does. Fiction creates emotional engagement and vivid experience. Informational text builds understanding and knowledge. A reader chooses based on their purpose.
